spacing.rule: A Year 3 word returns in the next lesson, three lessons later, a unit later and a unit and a half later. Where that falls past lesson 36 it is carried into Year 4 (outline recycled_words_by_lesson). Each lesson has at least 6 recycled words once 6 exist.

sounds.teacher_tip: Short and open, mouth wide, like the a in father said quickly. Never ay as in say.
Pure and round. Do not slide into ow: no rhymes with nothing in English, keep the lips still.
Like the e in bed. Never ee and never silent, even at the end of a word.
Like ee in see, but short and clean.
Like oo in moon, short. Never you.
Most speakers in Spain and Latin America say ll like the y in yes. In parts of Argentina and Uruguay it sounds like sh. Accept both; model the y.
As in English church. One of the few sounds English children already have.
Like the ny in canyon. The squiggle is called a tilde; without it the word changes.
A hard k sound, with no puff of air after it.
In Castilian Spanish ce and ci sound like th in think. In Latin America, the Canaries and parts of Andalucía they sound like s (seseo). Both are correct; we model Castilian and accept s.
The same sound as ce and ci: th in think in Castilian, s in Latin America. Spanish writes ce and ci but za, zo, zu.
The u is silent: que sounds like ke, qui like ki.
The h is never said. Hola starts with the o.
In Spanish v and b make the same sound. At the start of a word both sound like English b. Children ask with b de burro or v de vaca when spelling.
A breathy sound from the back of the throat, like ch in the Scottish loch. Softer, more like h, in the Caribbean, the Canaries and much of Latin America.
A hard g as in got.
Before e and i, g makes the same sound as j. Pair it with j words so children see the link.
One quick tap of the tongue, like the tt in butter said fast in an American accent.

sounds.grapheme: rr, and r at the start
sounds.teacher_tip: A rolled r, several taps. An r at the start of a word, or after n, l or s, is rolled too. Pero (but) and perro (dog) are a lovely pair to contrast.
Two vowels glide into one beat: we as in wet.
Two vowels glide into one beat: ye as in yes.
Before a vowel y sounds like y in yes, the same as ll for most speakers (yeísmo). On its own, y (and) sounds like ee.
At the end of a word y is a vowel and glides: hay sounds like eye, soy like soy sauce, muy like mwee.
The written accent tells you which part of the word to say loudest. It never changes the vowel sound.
The u is silent and keeps the g hard: gui sounds like gee in geese.
Cu before another vowel sounds like kw, as in quick. Compare que, where the u is silent.
Words ending in a vowel, n or s stress the next to last part (MEsa). Other words stress the last part (profeSOR). An accent breaks the rule (LÁpiz).
Between vowels d softens, close to th in this. At the start of a word it is a clear d.
Between vowels b and v soften: the lips nearly touch but do not close.
The two dots (diéresis) tell you to say the u: pingüino, not pinguino.
Usually ks. In México and a few place names it sounds like j.
The first c is k, the second is the th sound (s in Latin America).
The r after a consonant is one quick tap. Practise tres slowly, then fast.
Each pair glides into one beat. Agua sounds like ahgwa, two beats not three.
The accent on í splits the vowels into two beats: dí a. Compare familia, where ia glides into one.
Letter names for spelling and dictation: a, be, ce, de, e, efe. Spain says uve for v; much of Latin America says ve corta.

grammar.point: ¡ ! and ¿ ?: a question or an exclamation opens with an upside down mark
grammar.teacher_explanation: Spanish shows a question or an exclamation from its first word, so a reader knows how to say it before starting. Write both marks every time.

grammar.point: me llamo and te llamas: me for I, te for you
grammar.teacher_explanation: Teach both as chunks. Point out that the ending changes with the person: llamo for me, llamas for you. This is the first glimpse of verb endings.

grammar.point: estoy as a chunk for how I feel
grammar.teacher_explanation: Estoy bien, estoy mal. Do not explain ser and estar yet; the chunk carries it. Children notice later that soy and estoy both mean I am.

grammar.point: no goes in front of the verb
grammar.teacher_explanation: English says I am not; Spanish says I not am. One word, no, before the verb makes any sentence negative.

grammar.point: A question can be a sentence said with a rising voice
grammar.teacher_explanation: Spanish often keeps the same words and only lifts the voice at the end. The written marks ¿ ? show it.

grammar.point: soy and tengo: I am and I have; age uses tengo
grammar.teacher_explanation: Spanish says I have eight years, not I am eight. A classic error in both directions, so say it aloud: tengo ocho años.

grammar.point: Every noun is masculine or feminine: un and una
grammar.teacher_explanation: Nouns have a gender, even objects. Un goes with masculine nouns, una with feminine. Learn the noun with its un or una, like a surname.

grammar.point: el and la mean the
grammar.teacher_explanation: El with masculine, la with feminine. Most nouns ending in o are masculine and most ending in a are feminine, with exceptions met later (el día).

grammar.point: hay means there is and there are
grammar.teacher_explanation: One word, never changes, whether one thing or many. ¿Qué hay? asks what is there.

grammar.point: Colours go after the noun
grammar.teacher_explanation: English says a red book; Spanish says a book red. Most adjectives follow the noun.

grammar.point: Adjectives agree: rojo becomes roja with a feminine noun
grammar.teacher_explanation: Adjectives ending in o change to a for feminine nouns. Adjectives ending in another letter (azul, verde, grande) stay the same.

grammar.point: Plurals: add s or es; los and las
grammar.teacher_explanation: After a vowel add s (libros). After a consonant add es (profesores). El and la become los and las.

grammar.point: mi means my
grammar.teacher_explanation: Mi does not change for masculine or feminine: mi padre, mi madre.

grammar.point: tiene: he or she has; su: his or her
grammar.teacher_explanation: Su does not show whose: su hermano can be his brother or her brother. Context tells you.

grammar.point: mis: my for more than one
grammar.teacher_explanation: Mi adds s with a plural noun: mis hermanos, mis libros. Tu and su do the same.

grammar.point: Numbers 16 to 19 are built from diez y
grammar.teacher_explanation: Dieciséis is diez y seis squeezed into one word. Spotting the parts makes 16 to 19 easy, and the same pattern returns at 21 (veintiuno).

grammar.point: ¿Tienes...? and no tengo
grammar.teacher_explanation: Ask with tienes and a rising voice. After no tengo the un is usually dropped: no tengo perro.

grammar.point: es plus an adjective that agrees
grammar.teacher_explanation: Es means he, she or it is, for what something is like. The adjective agrees with the noun: mi perro es pequeño.

grammar.point: me gusta plus el or la
grammar.teacher_explanation: Spanish keeps the article after me gusta: me gusta el pan, not me gusta pan. No me gusta for the negative.

grammar.point: pero joins two ideas that pull different ways
grammar.teacher_explanation: Use pero to join a like and a dislike into one longer sentence.
examples: Me gusta el pan pero no me gusta la leche.

grammar.point: me gustan with more than one thing
grammar.teacher_explanation: Gusta becomes gustan when the thing liked is plural, because the thing does the pleasing.

grammar.point: me gusta plus a verb ending in ar, er or ir
grammar.teacher_explanation: The verb stays in its dictionary form (the infinitive). Children spot the endings ar, er, ir.

grammar.point: mucho after the verb, muy before an adjective
grammar.teacher_explanation: Both make things stronger. Mucho goes with gustar; muy goes before a describing word.

grammar.point: porque gives a reason
grammar.teacher_explanation: Porque plus es plus an adjective gives a reason: porque es divertido. One word, no accent.
examples: Me gusta leer porque es divertido.
No me gusta cantar porque no es divertido.

grammar.point: Days have no capital letter; el lunes means on Monday
grammar.teacher_explanation: Days are masculine and written in lower case. El lunes means on Monday, with no word for on.

grammar.point: Hoy es plus a day
grammar.teacher_explanation: Es links today and the day: hoy es lunes.
examples: ¿Hoy es domingo? No, hoy es lunes.

grammar.point: Weather with hace: hace sol, hace frío
grammar.teacher_explanation: Spanish says it makes sun. ¿Qué tiempo hace? asks what the weather is like.

grammar.point: llueve stands alone; hace calor, hace viento
grammar.teacher_explanation: Llueve is a verb on its own: no hace in front. The others take hace.

grammar.point: cuando joins the weather to what I do; a plus el becomes al
grammar.teacher_explanation: Cuando starts the first idea, a comma, then the second idea. A plus el always joins to make al.
examples: Cuando hace sol, voy al parque.
Cuando llueve, no voy al parque.
Cuando hace frío, me gusta leer.

grammar.point: tu means your; tú means you
grammar.teacher_explanation: The accent is the only difference. ¿Cuál es tu...? asks what your favourite is.
examples: Mi día favorito es el sábado.

grammar.point: está for where something is
grammar.teacher_explanation: Está answers ¿dónde?: where something is. Es says what it is like. Introduced here, contrasted in lesson 4 of this unit.
examples: El libro está en la mesa.

grammar.point: con means with
grammar.teacher_explanation: Con plus a person or a thing. Note con mi amigo, con mi familia.
examples: Voy al parque con mi amigo.

grammar.point: estoy and está with feelings
grammar.teacher_explanation: Feelings use estar: estoy feliz, está triste. Feliz and triste do not change for masculine or feminine.

grammar.point: es or está: what something is like, or where it is and how it feels
grammar.teacher_explanation: Es for what someone or something is like. Está for where it is and how it feels right now. The first explicit contrast; it returns every year.

grammar.point: Joining words: y, pero, porque, cuando
grammar.teacher_explanation: The four joining words of Year 3 turn short sentences into a longer one. Children choose and say aloud.
examples: Me gusta el parque porque es divertido.

grammar.point: My key verbs: soy, tengo, estoy, hay, me gusta, voy
grammar.teacher_explanation: An end of year map of the six verb chunks children own. Sorting them shows which mean I and which do not.
examples: Soy Pebble y tengo ocho años.
Me gusta el sábado porque voy al parque.

grammar.point: ser in the singular: soy, eres, es
grammar.teacher_explanation: The three singular forms of to be (what someone is like). Endings show the person.

grammar.point: tener in the singular: tengo, tienes, tiene
grammar.teacher_explanation: The three singular forms of to have, and age with tener.

grammar.point: vivir: vivo en, vives en
grammar.teacher_explanation: Where I live: vivo en plus a town. The first er or ir verb children own.

grammar.point: hay and no hay; no hay drops un
grammar.teacher_explanation: No hay parque, no hay cine. Hay plus un for one thing, plus a number for more.
examples: En mi pueblo hay un parque.

grammar.point: voy a plus al or a la
grammar.teacher_explanation: A plus el makes al; a la stays two words.

grammar.point: estar in the singular: estoy, estás, está
grammar.teacher_explanation: Feelings and location in all three singular forms.

grammar.point: tener for how the body feels: tengo frío, tengo hambre
grammar.teacher_explanation: Spanish says I have cold, I have hunger. A set of chunks with tener.

grammar.point: quiero plus a noun or a verb
grammar.teacher_explanation: Quiero is I want. With por favor it makes a polite request.

grammar.point: Numbers 21 to 100 by tens and with y
grammar.teacher_explanation: Veintiuno to veintinueve are one word; from treinta y uno the y stays separate.

grammar.point: Regular ar verbs in the singular: hablo, hablas, habla
grammar.teacher_explanation: Take off ar and add o, as, a. The pattern unlocks hundreds of verbs.

grammar.point: How often: siempre, a veces, nunca
grammar.teacher_explanation: Frequency words go before the verb. Nunca can stand alone before the verb.

grammar.point: Telling the time: es la una, son las dos
grammar.teacher_explanation: Es for one o'clock, son for the rest, because the hours are plural.

grammar.point: Parts of the day: por la mañana, por la tarde, por la noche
grammar.teacher_explanation: Por la mañana means in the morning. Mañana alone means tomorrow.
examples: Por la mañana voy al colegio.

grammar.point: Regular ar verbs, all six persons, present
grammar.teacher_explanation: o, as, a, amos, áis, an. Vosotros is Spain; Latin America uses ustedes for the plural you.

grammar.point: Opinions with porque plus es or son
grammar.teacher_explanation: Es with one thing, son with more than one: las matemáticas son difíciles.
examples: Me gusta el inglés porque es fácil.
No me gusta porque es aburrido.

grammar.point: estar for location, all persons
grammar.teacher_explanation: Estoy, estás, está, estamos, estáis, están. Where people and things are.
examples: La cocina está al lado del salón.

grammar.point: Prepositions of place: cerca de, al lado de, delante de, detrás de
grammar.teacher_explanation: De plus el makes del.
examples: Mi casa está cerca del parque.
El perro está detrás de la puerta.
Al lado de mi casa hay un parque.

grammar.point: ir in the present: voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van
grammar.teacher_explanation: The most frequent irregular verb pattern after ser and estar.

grammar.point: ir a plus a verb: the near future
grammar.teacher_explanation: Voy a jugar means I am going to play. The first way to talk about the future.
examples: El sábado vamos a ir a la playa.

grammar.point: Comparisons: más que, menos que
grammar.teacher_explanation: Más alto que means taller than. The adjective still agrees.
examples: El elefante es más grande que el perro.
La tortuga es menos rápida que el gato.
Mi hermana es más alta que yo.

grammar.point: Adjective agreement in all four forms
grammar.teacher_explanation: Masculine, feminine, singular, plural: blanco, blanca, blancos, blancas.

grammar.point: Regular er and ir verbs in the present
grammar.teacher_explanation: Como, comes, come; vivo, vives, vive. The two other verb families.

grammar.point: Negatives: nunca, nada, no ... ni
grammar.teacher_explanation: Spanish keeps no before the verb and adds nunca or nada after: no como nada.
examples: No me gusta ni la carne ni el pescado.

grammar.point: Possessives with plurals: mis, tus, sus, nuestro
grammar.teacher_explanation: Nuestro agrees in four forms: nuestro, nuestra, nuestros, nuestras.

grammar.point: Question words: qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cómo, cuánto, por qué
grammar.teacher_explanation: All carry an accent when they ask. Questions open with ¿.

grammar.point: The past as chunks: fui, fue, visité, comí
grammar.teacher_explanation: I went and it was first, then the regular é and í endings for I.

grammar.point: Past time markers: ayer, el fin de semana pasado, el verano pasado
grammar.teacher_explanation: A time phrase at the start tells the listener a past tense is coming.
examples: El fin de semana pasado jugué al fútbol.

grammar.point: querer and poder plus a verb
grammar.teacher_explanation: Quiero comer, puedo cocinar. Stem changes e to ie and o to ue.

grammar.point: Words that change across the Spanish speaking world
grammar.teacher_explanation: Patata and papa, zumo and jugo, coche and carro. Both are right; context decides.

grammar.point: llevar plus clothes, with colour agreement
grammar.teacher_explanation: Llevo una camiseta roja. The colour agrees with the clothes.
examples: Mi hermano lleva unos vaqueros negros.

grammar.point: este and esta: this
grammar.teacher_explanation: Este with masculine, esta with feminine; estos and estas in the plural.

grammar.point: Stem changing verbs: juego, prefiero, puedo
grammar.teacher_explanation: Inside the verb, u becomes ue, e becomes ie, o becomes ue, except for nosotros and vosotros.
examples: No puedo usar el móvil en clase.

grammar.point: Opinions with creo que and pienso que
grammar.teacher_explanation: I think that, plus a sentence. A step toward giving and defending a view.
examples: Pienso que los videojuegos son divertidos.

grammar.point: me gustaría plus a verb: I would like
grammar.teacher_explanation: Polite and future facing: me gustaría ser, me gustaría visitar.

grammar.point: quiero ser plus a job, with no un
grammar.teacher_explanation: Spanish drops the article with jobs: quiero ser profesor.

grammar.point: Three time frames in one paragraph
grammar.teacher_explanation: Fui (past), voy (present), voy a (future) side by side, the bridge into Year 7.
examples: El año pasado fui a Madrid.
El año que viene voy a ir al instituto.

From llamarse. Taught as a chunk.
Taught as a chunk. Literally how do you call yourself.
Friendly and very common in Spain and Latin America.

With an accent when it asks a question.

Feminine negra.

Children also say mamá.

words.english: he is, she is, it is
words.note: From ser.
The same for masculine and feminine.
Feminine pequeña.

words.english: his name is, her name is, its name is
words.note: From llamarse, like me llamo.
Literally it pleases me. Use with one thing or with a verb.
Feminine, but el agua, because the word starts with a stressed a.

tú for a friend or a child. Usted is the polite form, met later. Without an accent, tu means your.
Also the colour orange in Spain.
Jugar al fútbol: play football. Infinitive; I play is juego (Year 4).

¿Qué tiempo hace? means what is the weather like.
Hace frío: it is cold. Also an adjective later: el agua está fría.
Hace calor: it is hot.
Hace viento: it is windy.

words.english: he is, she is, it is (where, how)
words.note: From estar, like estoy.
En casa means at home.
A girl friend is una amiga.

units.title: Hello, who I am
units.context: Meeting someone new: greetings, my name, how I feel, numbers 1 to 10 and my age. Planet Friends Bloop and Pebble meet the class.

lessons.title: ¡Hola!
i_can: I can say hello and goodbye in Spanish.
I can answer yes or no.
I can say the Spanish a and o sounds.
lessons.speaking_task: Walk and greet: children move round the room, meet a partner, say ¡Hola! with a wave, then ¡Adiós! and move on.
lessons.story_or_chant: Chant with a clap on each word: "¡Hola, hola, buenos días! ¡Adiós, adiós!"

lessons.title: Me llamo
i_can: I can say my name in Spanish.
I can ask a friend their name.
I can hear the difference between e and i.
lessons.speaking_task: Name chain: each child asks the next ¿Cómo te llamas? and answers Me llamo plus their name.
lessons.story_or_chant: Call and response with a puppet: "¿Cómo te llamas? Me llamo Bloop. ¡Hola, Bloop!"

lessons.title: ¿Qué tal?
i_can: I can ask how someone is.
I can say I am well or not well.
I can say thank you.
lessons.speaking_task: Feelings thumbs: the teacher asks ¿Qué tal?; children answer with thumbs and the words estoy bien or estoy mal.
lessons.story_or_chant: Chant, quiet then loud: "¿Qué tal? ¿Qué tal? Estoy bien, gracias. ¿Qué tal? Estoy mal."

lessons.title: Uno, dos, tres
i_can: I can count from 1 to 5 in Spanish.
I can say no in front of a word to make it not.
I can say the ll sound in me llamo.
lessons.speaking_task: Show me: the teacher says a number, children show it on their fingers and say it back.
lessons.story_or_chant: Counting rhyme with a jump on cinco: "Uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco. ¡Hola, hola, hola!"

lessons.title: Seis, siete, ocho
i_can: I can count from 6 to 10 in Spanish.
I can ask a question with my voice going up.
I can say the ch sound in ocho.
lessons.speaking_task: Guess my number: a partner asks ¿Ocho? and the other answers sí or no, nueve.
lessons.story_or_chant: Counting rhyme up and down: "Seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez. ¡Diez! ¡Diez! ¡Adiós!"

lessons.title: Tengo ocho años
i_can: I can say how old I am.
I can ask a friend how old they are.
I can introduce myself in three short sentences.
lessons.speaking_task: Introduce yourself to the class: Hola, soy plus name, tengo plus age, adiós.
lessons.story_or_chant: Bloop introduces itself, the class copies with their own name: "Hola, soy Bloop. Tengo siete años. ¡Adiós!"

units.title: In my classroom
units.context: Things around the classroom, used to learn that every noun is masculine or feminine, how to say a and the, colours after the noun, and there is.

lessons.title: Un libro, una mesa
i_can: I can name a book and a table in Spanish.
I can sort words into un words and una words.
I can use un and una.
lessons.speaking_task: Point and say: the teacher points to an object, children say un libro or una mesa, and stand up for una.
lessons.story_or_chant: Rhythm chant: "Un libro, un libro. Una mesa, una mesa. ¡Uno, dos, tres!"

lessons.title: La puerta
i_can: I can name a door and a chair.
I can use el and la for the.
I can say the Spanish ci sound in cinco.
lessons.speaking_task: Label hunt: pairs read word cards and stick el or la labels on real objects, reading each one aloud.
lessons.story_or_chant: Touch and say chant: "La mesa, la silla, la puerta, el libro. ¡Uno, dos, tres, cuatro!"

lessons.title: ¿Qué hay?
i_can: I can say what there is using hay.
I can ask ¿Qué hay?
I can say the z sound in diez.
lessons.speaking_task: Mystery bag: a partner feels inside and asks ¿Qué hay?; the other answers Hay un bolígrafo or Hay un libro.
lessons.story_or_chant: Question and answer chant: "¿Qué hay? ¿Qué hay? Hay un libro. ¿Qué hay? ¿Qué hay? Hay un bolígrafo."

lessons.title: Rojo, azul, verde
i_can: I can say three colours in Spanish.
I can put the colour after the thing.
I can read que and qui with a silent u.
lessons.speaking_task: Colour describe: a child holds up an object and says un libro rojo; the class repeats if it is right.
lessons.story_or_chant: Colour song: "Rojo, rojo, un libro rojo. Azul, azul, una mesa azul. Verde, verde, un bolígrafo verde."

lessons.title: Una silla roja
i_can: I can change rojo to roja for a girl word.
I can describe a thing in my classroom.
I can write a short phrase from memory.
lessons.speaking_task: Describe and draw: one partner says una silla roja, the other draws it, then they swap.
lessons.story_or_chant: Chant: "La clase, la clase: una silla roja, una mesa blanca, un libro negro."

lessons.title: Los libros
i_can: I can make a word plural.
I can use los and las.
I can find a new word in a picture dictionary.
lessons.speaking_task: Count the class: pairs count real objects and say Hay tres libros, Hay cinco sillas.
lessons.story_or_chant: Counting chant: "Uno, dos, tres: los libros. Cuatro, cinco, seis: las sillas. ¡Siete, ocho, nueve, diez!"

units.title: My family and my pets
units.context: Who is in my family and what pets we have, used to learn have, my, his or her, describing with es, and numbers to 20.

lessons.title: Mi familia
i_can: I can name my mother and father in Spanish.
I can say my with mi.
I can say the j sound.
lessons.speaking_task: Family photo: children show a drawing and say mi madre, mi padre, pointing to each.
lessons.story_or_chant: Chant: "Mi madre, mi padre, mi familia. ¡Uno, dos, tres! ¡Hola, familia!"

lessons.title: Mi hermano
i_can: I can say brother and sister.
I can say what someone has with tiene.
I can use su for his or her.
lessons.speaking_task: Find someone who: children ask and answer about brothers and sisters, then report Bloop tiene un hermano.
lessons.story_or_chant: Chant: "Tengo un hermano. Tengo una hermana. ¿Y Bloop? Bloop tiene un hermano."

lessons.title: Once a quince
i_can: I can count from 11 to 15.
I can use mis for more than one.
I can say ge and gi like j.
lessons.speaking_task: Number bingo: the caller says the numbers, players cover them, and the winner reads the numbers back to check.
lessons.story_or_chant: Rhyme: "Once, doce, trece, catorce, quince. ¡Quince! ¡Quince! ¡Adiós!"

lessons.title: Dieciséis a veinte
i_can: I can count from 16 to 20.
I can see diez and seis inside dieciséis.
I can tap a single r.
lessons.speaking_task: Count around the circle from one to twenty and back; a mistake starts again at uno.
lessons.story_or_chant: Counting rap: "Dieciséis, diecisiete, dieciocho, diecinueve, ¡veinte!"

lessons.title: Mi perro
i_can: I can name a dog, a cat and a bird.
I can ask a friend ¿Tienes un perro?
I can roll the rr in perro.
lessons.speaking_task: Pet survey: children ask three friends ¿Tienes un perro? and tally the answers.
lessons.story_or_chant: Question chant: "¿Tienes un perro? ¡Sí! ¿Tienes un gato? ¡No! ¿Tienes un pájaro? ¡Sí, sí, sí!"

lessons.title: Mi gato es pequeño
i_can: I can say what my pet is like.
I can say my pet's name.
I can write two sentences about a pet from memory.
lessons.speaking_task: Pet show: each child presents a real or made up pet in two sentences to a small group.
lessons.story_or_chant: Mini poem: "Mi perro es grande. Mi gato es pequeño. Mi pájaro se llama Pebble."

units.title: What I like
units.context: Food and play as context for opinions: I like and I do not like, and, but, because.

lessons.title: Me gusta
i_can: I can say I like a food.
I can say I do not like a food.
I can say ie in bien and siete.
lessons.speaking_task: Thumbs vote: the teacher holds up a food card; children say me gusta or no me gusta with a gesture.
lessons.story_or_chant: Chant: "Me gusta el pan, me gusta el pan. ¡No, no, no! No me gusta la leche."

lessons.title: ¿Y tú?
i_can: I can ask ¿Te gusta?
I can join two ideas with pero.
I can say y and yo.
lessons.speaking_task: Opinion ping pong: a partner says what they like and asks ¿y tú?; the other answers and asks back.
lessons.story_or_chant: Call and response: "¿Te gusta el pan? ¡Sí! ¿Y tú? Yo, no. ¡Me gusta la leche!"

lessons.title: Las naranjas
i_can: I can say I like more than one thing with me gustan.
I can name fruit and oranges.
I can say hay, soy and muy.
lessons.speaking_task: Fruit stall role play: children sort picture cards into me gusta and me gustan piles and say each aloud.
lessons.story_or_chant: Song: "Naranjas, naranjas, me gustan las naranjas. Fruta, fruta, me gusta la fruta."

lessons.title: Me gusta jugar
i_can: I can say I like to play or to sing.
I can spot verbs ending in ar, er and ir.
I can find the loud part of a word with an accent.
lessons.speaking_task: Mime and guess: one child mimes jugar or cantar, the class says Te gusta jugar.
lessons.story_or_chant: Action chant: "Me gusta cantar. Me gusta el fútbol. Me gusta jugar. ¿Y tú?"

lessons.title: Mucho
i_can: I can say I like something a lot.
I can use muy before a describing word.
I can say hard c and soft c.
lessons.speaking_task: Opinion line: children stand on a line from no me gusta to me gusta mucho and say their sentence.
lessons.story_or_chant: Chant: "Muy bien, muy bien, me gusta mucho. Leer, leer, me gusta leer."

lessons.title: Porque es divertido
i_can: I can give a reason with porque.
I can say also with también.
I can write a sentence with a reason from memory.
lessons.speaking_task: Opinion chain: each child adds a reason, porque es divertido, to a friend's me gusta sentence.
lessons.story_or_chant: Chant: "Me gusta jugar porque es divertido. ¿Y tú? ¡Yo también!"

units.title: My week and the weather
units.context: Days of the week and the weather, joined into longer sentences with when, and the first question about your favourite.

lessons.title: Los días
i_can: I can say the school days in Spanish.
I can write the days without a capital letter.
I can hear r and rr.
lessons.speaking_task: Day line up: five children hold day cards and the class puts them in order, saying each one.
lessons.story_or_chant: Days song: "Lunes, martes, miércoles, jueves, viernes. ¡Me gusta el viernes!"

lessons.title: Hoy es sábado
i_can: I can say all seven days.
I can say what day it is today.
I can say a silent h and a strong j.
lessons.speaking_task: Daily question: a helper asks the class what day it is and answers with Hoy es plus the day.
lessons.story_or_chant: Weekend chant: "Hoy es sábado. ¡Sí, sí, sí! Hoy es domingo. ¡Sí, sí, sí!"

lessons.title: ¿Qué tiempo hace?
i_can: I can ask what the weather is like.
I can say it is sunny or cold.
I can say the th sound in hace.
lessons.speaking_task: Weather reporter: a child looks out of the window and reports Hoy hace sol or Hoy hace frío.
lessons.story_or_chant: Weather chant with actions: "¿Qué tiempo hace? ¿Qué tiempo hace? ¡Hace sol! ¡Hace frío!"

lessons.title: Llueve
i_can: I can say it is raining.
I can say it is hot or windy.
I can say ll and y the same way.
lessons.speaking_task: Weather map: children read a weather card and say it to the class like a forecaster.
lessons.story_or_chant: Rain rhyme: "Llueve, llueve. Hace viento. Hace calor. ¡Hace sol!"

lessons.title: Cuando hace sol
i_can: I can join the weather to what I do with cuando.
I can say I go to the park.
I can say ue and ie.
lessons.speaking_task: Weather and plans: a partner names the weather and the other answers with a cuando sentence.
lessons.story_or_chant: Chant: "Cuando hace sol, voy al parque. Cuando llueve, ¡no, no, no!"

lessons.title: Mi día favorito
i_can: I can ask what your favourite day is.
I can tell the class my favourite day and why.
I can write my favourite day from memory.
lessons.speaking_task: Class survey: children ask ¿Cuál es tu día favorito?, then one presents the class result.
lessons.story_or_chant: Rhyme: "¿Cuál es tu día favorito? Mi día favorito es el sábado, porque voy al parque."

units.title: Our story
units.context: ¿Dónde está Bloop? A decodable story built only from known words, read aloud, performed, then the end of year check.

lessons.title: ¿Dónde está Bloop?
i_can: I can ask where someone is.
I can read the first page of our story.
I can say where something is with en.
lessons.speaking_task: Hide and find: a toy is hidden; children ask ¿Dónde está? and guess ¿Está en la mesa?
lessons.story_or_chant: Story page 1: "Hoy es sábado. Hace sol. ¿Dónde está Bloop? ¿Está en la casa? No."

lessons.title: Con Orbit
i_can: I can say who I am with using con.
I can read the second page of our story aloud.
I can say mira to point something out.
lessons.speaking_task: Read in pairs: one reads a sentence, the other points to the picture that matches.
lessons.story_or_chant: Story page 2: "Pebble está en el parque con Orbit. ¡Mira! Hay un perro. ¿Es Bloop? No."

lessons.title: Feliz, triste
i_can: I can say how someone feels.
I can read a page of the story with feeling in my voice.
I can use ahora for now.
lessons.speaking_task: Feelings faces: the teacher reads a sentence; children show a happy or sad face and repeat it.
lessons.story_or_chant: Story page 3: "Pebble está triste. ¿Dónde está Bloop? ¿Está en la clase? No."

lessons.title: ¡Vamos!
i_can: I can tell es and está apart.
I can read speech in a speech bubble.
I can read the end of our story.
lessons.speaking_task: Who said it: children read a speech bubble and say who says it, dice Orbit or dice Pebble.
lessons.story_or_chant: Story page 4: "«¡Mira!», dice Orbit. «¡Bloop está aquí!» Ahora Pebble está feliz. «¡Vamos!»"

lessons.title: Escucha y repite
i_can: I can read our whole story aloud.
I can perform the story to an audience.
I can use joining words to make a longer sentence.
lessons.speaking_task: Performance: groups act the story for another class, each child reading one line clearly.
lessons.story_or_chant: Whole story, with echo reading: "Escucha y repite: ¡Bloop está aquí! ¡Vamos al parque! Fin."

lessons.title: ¡Muy bien!
i_can: I can ask how to say a word in Spanish.
I can say I do not know and ask again.
I can show what I know in the end of year check.
lessons.speaking_task: End of year check: a short talk with a partner about name, age, family, likes and the weather.
lessons.story_or_chant: Year 3 rap: "¿Cómo se dice dog? ¡Perro! ¿Otra vez? ¡Perro! No sé, no sé. ¡Sí, sé! ¡Muy bien!"

outline.title: Me and you
outline.context: Introductions in more depth: what I am like, who I live with, where I live. Dictation starts this unit.

outline.title: My town
outline.context: Places in my town, what there is and is not, and going to places.

outline.title: My body and how I feel
outline.context: Body, feelings and how the body feels (hungry, cold), with estar opened up.

outline.title: At the market
outline.context: Food shopping role play: what I want, please, numbers to 100 and prices in euros.

outline.title: Sport and hobbies
outline.context: What I do and how often, with the first regular verb pattern in the singular.

outline.title: A day in my life
outline.context: Telling the time and parts of the day, ending in a Year 4 reader and performance.

outline.title: My school day
outline.context: School subjects and opinions with reasons, and ar verbs in all six persons.

outline.title: My home
outline.context: Rooms and where things are, with estar for location and prepositions.

outline.title: Weekend plans
outline.context: Going out and what I am going to do: ir and the near future.

outline.title: Animals and our planet
outline.context: Animals from Spain and Latin America compared, with comparatives and full agreement.

outline.title: Healthy me
outline.context: Food, drink and routines with er and ir verbs, and negatives.

outline.title: Our Year 5 play
outline.context: A short play written by the class from known language, possessives and the full set of question words.

outline.title: Holidays
outline.context: Where I went and what it was like: the past tense as chunks, then the regular I forms.

outline.title: Food across the Spanish speaking world
outline.context: Dishes and words from Spain and Latin America, with querer and poder plus a verb.

outline.title: What I wear
outline.context: Clothes and colours with full agreement, llevar, and this and these.

outline.title: Digital me
outline.context: Screens, games and being online in Spanish: what I use, how often and what I think about it. Ties to the Guided Childhood thread.

outline.title: When I grow up
outline.context: Jobs and hopes with me gustaría and quiero ser.

outline.title: Ready for Year 7
outline.context: A paragraph in three time frames, a final reader, and the transition record for secondary.
